As a new mom, I was curious about what those articles had to say. I painstakingly read them both in their entirety, and have archived them in case you want to suffer through them as well: 9 Common Mistakes Parents Make About Their Kid's Weight and What I Teach My Son When I Say I Am Fat: Practicing Self Love for Our Children’s Sake

The first one is long-winded and very stupid. It pretty much suggests that talking to your child about healthy weight goals, healthy eating habits, or healthy exercise habits is a form of abuse. The whole thing is awful, but the last point, "Missing the opportunity to see weight as one more aspect of diversity" suggests that instead of talking to your child about healthy behaviours, that you should "let your children know that, weight is a characteristic, not a behavior." It goes on further to suggest:

Just like they don’t get to decide how short or tall they’ll grow to be, or the color of their skin or eyes, they don’t get to choose their weight range.

I can agree nobody gets to choose their "weight range". I'm 5'7", so a healthy BMI for me would be between 118 and 159. I didn't get to choose those exact numbers. I didn't say, "a healthy BMI for me is between 118 pounds and 159 pounds" because it goes based on height, which I also didn't get to choose. But I do choose to stay within those two numbers. If I was a stupid ham, I could choose to be in the overweight or obese ranges for my height based on what I ate and how much. So you might not get to choose the exact numbers for each range (underweight, healthy, overweight, obese, etc.) but you can definitely choose which category you are in.

The second article, even though it was shorter, was just as cringeworthy as the first. I wanted to read it because I'm a new mom of a baby boy, and I have every intention on raising him as a little shitlord. It pretty much says that by showing your child you are not happy with your own body, such as when you say, "I look fat and ugly", you are teaching him the following, which the article indicates are bad lessons:
